The Korean alphabet is the modern writing system for the Korean language. It has gone by a variety of names, such as Chosŏn'gŭl[a] in North Korea, Hangul[b] internationally, and Hangeul[c] in South Korea. The script's original name was Hunminjeongeum.[d]

Before Hangul's creation, Korea had been using Hanja (Chinese characters) since antiquity. As Hanja was poorly suited for representing the Korean language, and because its difficulty contributed to high illiteracy, Joseon king Sejong the Great (r. 1418–1450) moved to create Hangul. The script was announced around late 1443 to early 1444 and officially published in 1446 via the text Hunminjeongeum and its companion commentary Hunminjeongeum Haerye. While Hangul saw gradual adoption among both the elite and commoners, it was looked down upon by the elite for centuries. It only began to receive societal acceptance in the late 19th century. It is now the predominant script for Korean in both Koreas and among the Korean diaspora. It is also used to write the Jeju language, and to a limited degree, the Cia-Cia language of Indonesia.

Hangul orthography has changed over time and differs between North and South Korea. Modern Korean language orthographies use 24[e] basic letters, which are called jamo. The 14 consonants can be combined amongst themselves to represent additional and composite sounds; the same principle applies for the 10 vowels. Such combinations yield 27 additional letters, resulting in a total of 51. They are arranged in syllable blocks consisting of an initial consonant, a vowel, and an optional final consonant. The syllables can be arranged in vertical or horizontal rows, although the latter practice has become dominant. Hangul punctuation is now largely similar to Western punctuation, with some differences. Spaces between words or phrases are a modern feature of Hangul.

Hangul letters were designed to be graphically simple, and traditionally consisted of only straight lines, dots, and circles. The shapes of five basic consonants are based on those of human speech organs. Most of the other basic consonants, which are considered to correspond to "harsher" sounds than those five, are derived by adding additional lines to those letters to indicate progressively harsher sounds. There are a number of other hypothesized inspirations for the letter shapes, but these are still debated.

The script has received significant praise from international linguists and historians. It is now a major point of pride for Korean people.

Namesedit
Main article: Names of the Korean alphabet

The Korean alphabet has been referred to by various names since its invention. Its original name was Hunminjeongeum (훈민정음; 訓民正音; Hunminjŏngŭm; 'Correct Sounds for the Instruction of the People'). It shared this name with the manuscript that introduced it.[1]

Internationally, the script goes by Hangul. This spelling has been adopted as a word in the English language[2] and is used by organizations like the International Organization for Standardization (which gives it the four-letter code Hang and numeric code 286).[3] Hangul is an ad-hoc romanization of the name South Korea uses for the script; South Korea's preferred Revised Romanization system renders this as Hangeul (한글). The McCune–Reischauer and related romanization systems render this as Han'gŭl. Without diacritics, this is rendered as Hangul. The name means script of Han, where Han is one of the names of Korea.[4] The name appeared some time around the early 1910s.[5][6]

In North Korea, the name Hangul was briefly used until it was replaced by Chosŏn'gŭl in 1949. This is in part due to differing preferences for names of Korea: North Korea refers to the whole of Korea as Chosŏn, while South Korea uses Hanguk.[7]

The script also went by various names with varying connotations as follows:

ŏnmun (언문; 諺文; 'vernacular script')[8] – the name used in contrast with chinmun (진문; 眞文; 'true script')[9] or chinsŏ (진서; 眞書; 'true writing') referring to Chinese characters and Classical Chinese[10].
panjŏl (반절; 反切)[11] – the Korean reading of the name of the Chinese linguistic system fanqie, which transcribes readings of Chinese characters by combining other Chinese characters. This name arose because some felt Hangul's design was similar to that of the system.[11]
kungmun (국문; 國文; 'national script')[12] – this name was used to portray Hangul as a national symbol.[10]
Classificationsedit

Hangul is a phonographic script: a writing system where graphemes represent the sounds of a language. It is also an alphabet.[13] The script is often described as "syllabic" because of how its letters are grouped into syllables (see § Syllable blocks),[14] although linguist John DeFrancis is skeptical of this.[15] Several linguists have instead argued for calling it an "alphabetic syllabary", "syllabic alphabet", or "alpha-syllabary".[16] While Hangul was originally a more phonemic script (where spelling is strictly tied to pronunciation), modern Hangul has become more morphophonemic (where some pronunciation changes are not reflected in spelling) over time (see Hangul orthography § Punch'ŏl vs. yŏnch'ŏl debate).[17]

Hangul and mixed script are considered to have a property called ŏnmun ilch'i (언문일치; 言文一致; lit. 'spoken–written agreement'): tight correspondence between pronunciation and text. By contrast, the Idu and Kugyŏl scripts for writing Korean do not have this property.[f][19] Pae, Winskel, and Kim argue this property was initially stronger but weakened over time due to changes in the language and script.[20]

Featural scriptedit

Some scholars argue that Hangul is what is called a "featural script": a writing system where the shapes of the symbols encode phonological features of the spoken language they represent. The term was coined by Sampson in a 1985 book, wherein he argued Hangul was featural. This argument is largely based on the Haerye's explanations for the derivations of the letter shapes.[21]

In a 1989 book, DeFrancis praises Hangul but questions Sampson's classification of Hangul as featural. He argues that Hangul encodes too few features of Korean and that most people literate in Hangul do not actively learn or process the featural principles used to construct the shapes of the letters.[22] In a 1997 book, Chin-Woo Kim rebuts DeFrancis's argument. He argues that DeFrancis relies on a count of Korean's features that is too high, and that other scholars provide lower counts. He also argues that, even if one accepts that most do not learn or perceive Hangul's featural aspects, that does not mean such aspects do not exist. Kim also claims that scholars argue Hangul is not a featural script because it does not neatly abide by Jakobsonian distinctive features.[23] In the same book, linguist Young-Key Kim-Renaud argues against a featural label. She argues it should be considered that the derivation rules are applied to varying quality and that some symbols represent or contribute to multiple significantly different sounds. Kim-Renaud gives the example of the dot: the dot is used as a vowel (ㆍ) and a component in other vowels (e.g. two of them in ㅑ). When used as a component, it does not carry the meaning of the dot vowel.[24] Linguists Pae, Winskel, and Kim argue that the featural designation is difficult to falsify, debatable, and uncertain.[25] Linguists Taylor and Taylor argue that not all of Hangul's letters are derived from articulatory features and their shape communicates little to learners and users of Korean.[26] Linguist Dimitrios Meletis feels that the label is given too much attention, and that the stroke addition rule and philosophical concepts behind the letters are not purely featural.[27]

Historyedit
Main article: History of Hangul
Backgroundedit

Before the invention of Hangul, Korea had been using Hanja (Chinese characters), since antiquity. The difficulty of the script limited its use to mostly upper-class people; commoners were largely illiterate.[28] Hanja is not well suited for representing the Korean language; the Chinese and Korean languages are not closely related and differ in significant ways.[29] Korean pronunciation and ideas could only be indirectly represented.[30]

Originedit
Main article: Origin of Hangul
First page of the Hunminjeongeum, which formally introduced Hangul

Due to a lack of records, it is unknown when work on Hangul first began, nor what that process looked like.[31] Joseon king Sejong the Great (r. 1418–1450) was responsible for Hangul's creation, and most scholars believe he was significantly personally involved in creating it.[32] Hangul was first introduced, likely in a mostly complete form, to Sejong's court in the 12th month of 1443 of the Korean calendar (around December 30, 1443 to January 28, 1444 in the Gregorian calendar).[33] Work then began on applying the script and developing official documentation for it. Part of this effort resulted in the creation of Yongbiŏch'ŏn'ga, the first ever piece of Hangul literature.[34]

In the 9th month of 1446 (the specific day of publication is not known), Hangul was officially promulgated via the introductory texts Hunminjeongeum and Hunminjeongeum Haerye.[35] The Hunminjeongeum begins with this now famous preface by Sejong:[36]

The sounds of our country's language are different from those of the Middle Kingdom and are not confluent with the sounds of characters. Therefore, among the ignorant people, there have been many who, having something they want to put into words, have in the end been unable to express their feelings. I have been distressed because of this, and have newly designed twenty-eight letters, which I wish to have everyone practice at their ease and make convenient for their daily use.[37]

— Sejong the Great, Hunminjeongeum, preface

Critics of Hangul emerged soon after its introduction. They argued that a native Korean script was too far a departure from Chinese civilization, which they insisted Korea should be deferent to in a Confucian manner.[38] Modern historians have argued that elitism and self-interest were other motivators for anti-Hangul elite; literacy in Hanja was then seen as a status symbol and general literacy was seen as potentially harming their social positions.[39]

Spreadedit
A copy of the landmark novel Hong Gildong jeon

While Sejong had attempted to spread Hangul throughout the government and society, his efforts had limited success.[40] Hangul was only rarely used during the 15th century; its use was largely centered in Seoul, among people close to the royal family and court.[41] It only began to spread outside of Seoul in the 16th century.[42] Women and Buddhists were significant early adopters of the script. While Hangul was rarely taught in traditional Confucianist curricula, it was often taught by women in the home.[43]

King Yeonsangun (r. 1495–1506) persecuted the use of Hangul during the Second Literati Purge of 1504 (갑자사화; 甲子士禍), after learning that criticisms of him had been written in the script.[44] In the 16th century, the government agency Bureau of Interpreters became a significant center for Hangul scholarship, with one of its members Ch'oe Sejin still being revered today for his lasting contributions to the script and Korean linguistics.[45]

Hangul orthography experienced significant changes in the script's early history. Around the time of Hangul's promulgation, an apparent dispute between whether to use a phonemic or morphophonemic orthography resulted in an apparent victory for the morphophonemic faction; among that faction was Sejong himself.[46] A number of letters gradually stopped seeing significant use by the late 16th century, including the base letters ㅿ and ㆆ.[47] By the 17th century, the letters ㅇ and ㆁ had merged into one.[48] Tone markings [ko] for Hangul stopped being used around the 16th century.[49] The chaotic 1592–1598 Imjin War caused significant disruption and inconsistencies to Hangul orthography that persisted and even worsened into the late 19th century.[50]

Hangul popular literature and sijo poetry began to flourish around the 17th century.[51] The landmark novel Hong Gildong jeon was published around the beginning of the century.[52]

Enlightenment and Korean Empire periodsedit
Tongnip sinmun, the first modern Korean newspaper and the first to use pure Hangul

With the end of Korea's isolationism in the 1870s, an influx of foreign ideas arrived in Korea. Around this time, Hangul began to be seen as a symbol of national identity and pride. Various Hangul reform movements arose, with many persisting into the late 20th century. Collectively, these efforts are referred to as the Hangul Movement [ko].[53] Various issues became debated, such as whether to use Hangul only or mixed script,[54] whether to abandon the syllable block structure and write linearly,[55] and whether to write vertically or horizontally.[56]

This era saw numerous landmark firsts for Hangul. Scottish missionary John Ross's landmark 1877 work Corean Primer (조선어 첫걸음) saw the introduction of spaces and horizontal writing for Hangul.[56] In 1888, a Morse code specification for Hangul was developed for the first time by Korean scholar Kim Hagu [ko].[57] In 1897, the first Braille encoding for Hangul, called Pyongyang Point (평양점자), was invented by Canadian missionary Rosetta Sherwood Hall.[58] This period also saw the rise of newspapers in Korea. In 1886, the Hansŏng chubo became the first Korean newspaper to use mixed script.[59] In 1896, The Independent, one of the earliest independent modern Korean newspapers, was established. It was written in pure Hangul.[60]

On 21 November 1894, the Joseon government decreed pure Hangul to be the country's preferred script for administrative documents, although mixed script was also allowed.[61] This edict was apparently enforced to varying degrees, as exclusive Hangul was rare in many documents even until the beginning of the colonial period.[62] Joseon was succeeded by the Korean Empire in 1897. On 19 July 1905, the Korean Empire approved the first official orthography for Hangul: the New Edition of National Writing (신정국문; 新訂國文).[63] Ultimately, this orthography proved controversial and was not put into significant practice.[64]

Colonial periodedit
Cover of the 1933 Unified Hangul Orthography

In 1910, Korea was colonized by the Empire of Japan. The Korean language and script saw varying degrees of repression during the colonial period.[65] After the 1919 March First Movement protests, the Japanese colonial government temporarily eased suppression of Korean culture in a phenomenon now dubbed cultural rule [ja; ko]. Hangul use and reform significantly expanded as a result.[66]

This period saw significant orthographic reform efforts. The colonial Government-General of Chōsen published the first Hangul orthography to be put in common practice in 1912 (revised in 1921 and 1930).[67] In 1933, the Korean Language Society (KLS) published its landmark Unified Hangul Orthography (UHO). # Hangul facts for kids

[Kids Encyclopedia Facts](https://kids.kiddle.co/)

[![Image 3: Hunmin jeong-eum](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/c/c7/Hunmin_jeong-eum.jpg/300px-Hunmin_jeong-eum.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Hunmin_jeong-eum.jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Hunmin_jeong-eum.jpg "Enlarge")

 A page from the _Hunmin Jeong-eum Eonhae_. The Hangul-only column, third from the left (나랏말ᄊᆞ미), has pitch-accent diacritics to the left of the syllable blocks.

**Hangul** or **Hangeul** ([Korean](link_4): 한글) is the special [alphabet](link_5) used to write the [Korean language](link_4). It's also used for the [Cia-Cia language](link_6) in parts of Indonesia.

King [Sejong the Great](link_7), who was the 4th King of the [Joseon Dynasty](link_8), created Hangul in 1443. It's still used by millions of people today! To help everyone learn Hangul, King Sejong published a book called _Hunminjeong'eum Haeryebon_. This important book was recognized by [UNESCO](link_9) in 1997 as a "Memory of the World." It explains exactly how Hangul was designed and how to use it.

The _Hunminjeong'eum Haeryebon_ book shares two main ideas behind Hangul's design. First, the shapes of the consonant letters look like the parts of your mouth and throat that you use to make those sounds. Second, the vowel letters are based on "Cheonji'in" (천지인). This refers to three basic ideas: the sky (천), the earth (지), and humans (인). Because of these clever design ideas, Hangul is known for being very easy to learn!

Even though Hangul was first mostly used by common people, it became the official writing system of Korea in the late 1800s. Today, it's the main way people write in both North and South Korea. [North Korea](link_10) uses only Hangul. In [South Korea](link_11), people mostly write in Hangul, but sometimes they still use older Chinese characters called Hanja.

## Contents

*   [Understanding Hangul Vowels](https://kids.kiddle.co/Hangul#Understanding_Hangul_Vowels)
*   [Exploring Hangul Consonants](https://kids.kiddle.co/Hangul#Exploring_Hangul_Consonants)
*   [How Hangul Forms Syllable Blocks](https://kids.kiddle.co/Hangul#How_Hangul_Forms_Syllable_Blocks)
*   [Examples of Hangul Words](https://kids.kiddle.co/Hangul#Examples_of_Hangul_Words)
*   [Images for kids](https://kids.kiddle.co/Hangul#Images_for_kids)
*   [See also](https://kids.kiddle.co/Hangul#See_also)

## Understanding Hangul Vowels

Vowels are letters like A, E, I, O, U. In Hangul, there are 21 vowel letters.

*   There are 10 simple vowels: ㅏㅓㅣㅑㅕ and ㅗㅜㅡㅛㅠ.
*   There are 11 more complex vowels, which are combinations of the simple ones: ㅐㅒㅔㅖ and ㅘㅙㅚㅝㅞㅟㅢ.

Here's what some of them mean:

ㅏ ㅓ ㅣ ㅑ ㅕ ㅗ ㅜ ㅡ ㅛ ㅠ ㅐ ㅒ ㅔ ㅖ ㅘ ㅙ ㅚ ㅝ ㅞ ㅟ ㅢ
a eo i ya yeo o u eu yo yu ae yae e ye wa wae oe wo we wi ui

If a vowel letter has two small lines, it usually means you add an extra "y" sound at the beginning when you say it.

## Exploring Hangul Consonants

Consonants are letters like B, G, L, M, N, S. Hangul has 14 simple consonant letters: ㄱㄴㄷㄹㅁㅂㅅㅇㅈㅊㅋㅌㅍㅎ.

Sometimes, these consonants can be written twice next to each other to make a slightly different sound.

Here's how some of them sound:

| Letter | Sound |
| --- | --- |
| Before a vowel | After a vowel |
| ㄱ | g | k |
| ㄴ | n |
| ㄷ | d | t |
| ㄹ | r | l |
| ㅁ | m |
| ㅂ | b | p |
| ㅅ | s | t |
| ㅇ | - | ng |
| ㅈ | j | t |
| ㅊ | ch | t |
| ㅋ | k |
| ㅌ | t |
| ㅍ | p |
| ㅎ | h | t |
| ㄲ | kk | k |
| ㄸ | tt | t |
| ㅃ | pp | p |
| ㅆ | ss | t |
| ㅉ | jj | t |

## How Hangul Forms Syllable Blocks

In Hangul, consonants and vowels are put together to form "blocks" that represent one syllable. A syllable is a single sound unit, like "han" in "Hangul" or "gul" in "Hangul."

These blocks are how Korean words are written. Here are some examples: 서울 한글 평양

## Examples of Hangul Words

Let's look at how some common Korean words are put together:

Seoul 서울 Hangul 한글 Pyongyang 평양
ㅅ ㅓ ㅇ ㅜ ㄹ ㅎ ㅏ ㄴ ㄱ ㅡ ㄹ ㅍ ㅕ ㅇ ㅇ ㅑ ㅇ
s eo-u l h a n g eu l p yeo ng-ya ng

**Seventeen** ([Korean](link_11):세븐틴), also known as **SVT**, is a popular South Korean [boy band](link_12). They were formed by Pledis Entertainment. The group has thirteen talented members: S.Coups, Jeonghan, Joshua, [Jun](link_8), Hoshi, Wonwoo, Woozi, DK, Mingyu, [The8](https://kids.kiddle.co/The8 "The8"), Seungkwan, Vernon, and Dino. Seventeen is special because they are a "self-producing" group. This means the members help write songs, create music, and even choreograph their dances.

Seventeen officially started on May 26, 2015, with their first mini-album, _17 Carat_. This album was very successful, staying on the US K-pop charts for a long time. It was also named one of the best K-pop albums of 2015 by _Billboard_. In 2023, their mini-albums _FML_ and _Seventeenth Heaven_ broke records for album sales. _FML_ became the best-selling album of 2023 worldwide. These achievements earned them the top "Album of the Year" award at the MAMA Awards in both 2023 and 2024.

The group performs together, but they also have three special teams: hip-hop, vocal, and performance. Each team focuses on a different skill. They also have several smaller groups called sub-units, like BSS, JxW, HxW, and CxM. Seventeen is famous for their amazing live shows and concert tours. Media outlets have called them "Performance Kings" and "Kings of Synchronization" because of their perfectly coordinated dances.

## What's in a Name?

The name "Seventeen" comes from a cool idea: "13 members + 3 teams + 1 group." This shows how their 13 members work in three different teams, but all come together as one amazing group. You might also see them called "SVT," which is a short way to say their name.

Their official fan club is called "Carat" ([Korean](link_11):캐럿). This name was announced in 2016. A carat is a unit used to measure diamonds. It's a nod to their first mini-album, _17 Carat_, and a song called "Shining Diamond." Seventeen has a global fan club on Weverse and a special one just for their fans in Japan.

## Seventeen's Journey: A Look at Their History

### Early Days and First Albums (2013–2016)

Before their official debut, Seventeen appeared on a show called _Seventeen TV_ starting in 2013. This show let fans see the trainees practicing and preparing. Right before their debut, they also starred in _Seventeen Project: Big Debut Plan_ in May 2015. This show shared their final steps to becoming a group.

[![Image 4: Seventeen (세븐틴) at 2015 Summer K-POP Festival](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/a/a6/Seventeen_%28%EC%84%B8%EB%B8%90%ED%8B%B4%29_at_2015_Summer_K-POP_Festival.jpg/300px-Seventeen_%28%EC%84%B8%EB%B8%90%ED%8B%B4%29_at_2015_Summer_K-POP_Festival.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Seventeen_(%EC%84%B8%EB%B8%90%ED%8B%B4)_at_2015_Summer_K-POP_Festival.jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Seventeen_(%EC%84%B8%EB%B8%90%ED%8B%B4)_at_2015_Summer_K-POP_Festival.jpg "Enlarge")

 Seventeen performing at the 2015 Summer K-pop Festival in Seoul.

Seventeen officially debuted on May 26, 2015, with a live TV showcase. A few days later, their first mini-album, _17 Carat_, came out. It was a big hit, becoming the longest-charting K-pop album of the year in the US. It was also the only new group's album to be on _Billboard'_ s "10 Best K-pop Albums of 2015" list.

On September 10, they released their second mini-album, _Boys Be_. This album became the best-selling album by a new group that year. Its success helped them win awards at major events like the Golden Disk Awards. Seventeen also held their first concert series in Seoul, called "Like Seventeen – Boys Wish," in December 2015.

Their first full studio album, _Love & Letter_, was released on April 25, 2016. The album did well in South Korea and Japan. They earned their first win on a music show with the song "Pretty U." Later that year, they went on their first concert tour, the Shining Diamonds Tour, visiting countries like Japan, Singapore, and Australia. On December 5, they released their third mini-album, _Going Seventeen_, with the song "Boom Boom."

### Global Recognition and Major Tours (2017–2020)

In 2017, Seventeen held a successful tour in Japan, even before their official debut there. Their fourth mini-album, _Al1_, was released on May 22. The song "Don't Wanna Cry" became one of their most famous songs. Its music video was the first for Seventeen to reach 200 million views on [YouTube](link_13). The group then went on their Diamond Edge tour, visiting cities across Asia and North America. On November 6, they released their second studio album, _Teen, Age_. In early 2018, _[Time](link_14)_ magazine recognized Seventeen as one of the top K-pop groups.

[![Image 5: Seventeen performing Don't Wanna Cry at Dream Concert 2017 02](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/2/26/Seventeen_performing_Don%27t_Wanna_Cry_at_Dream_Concert_2017_02.png/300px-Seventeen_performing_Don%27t_Wanna_Cry_at_Dream_Concert_2017_02.png)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Seventeen_performing_Don%27t_Wanna_Cry_at_Dream_Concert_2017_02.png)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Seventeen_performing_Don%27t_Wanna_Cry_at_Dream_Concert_2017_02.png "Enlarge")

 Seventeen performing "Don't Wanna Cry" at Dream Concert 2017.

Seventeen officially debuted in Japan on May 30, 2018, with their first Japanese mini-album, _We Make You_. They also released their fifth Korean mini-album, _You Make My Day_, with the song "Oh My!". This album was their first to be certified platinum in South Korea.

[![Image 6: 180716 Seveteen performing "Oh My!" at You Make My Day Showcase](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/e/e4/180716_Seveteen_performing_%22Oh_My%21%22_at_You_Make_My_Day_Showcase.png/300px-180716_Seveteen_performing_%22Oh_My%21%22_at_You_Make_My_Day_Showcase.png)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:180716_Seveteen_performing_%22Oh_My!%22_at_You_Make_My_Day_Showcase.png)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:180716_Seveteen_performing_%22Oh_My!%22_at_You_Make_My_Day_Showcase.png "Enlarge")

 Seventeen performing "Oh My!" at their You Make My Day Showcase in 2018.

Their sixth mini-album, _You Made My Dawn_, came out on January 21, 2019. The lead song "Home" won many awards on music shows. In May 2019, they released their first Japanese single album, "Happy Ending", which was very popular in Japan. Later that year, Seventeen announced their Ode to You World Tour. This tour included stops in Asia, North America, and Europe, though some shows were canceled in 2020. On September 16, they released their third studio album, _An Ode_. This album sold 700,000 copies in its first week and earned them their first "Daesang" (grand prize) for Album of the Year. _Billboard_ also called it the best K-pop album of the year.

### Contract Renewal and "Power of Love" (2020–2021)

On April 1, 2020, Seventeen released their second Japanese single, "Fallin' Flower". It quickly became number one on the Oricon Daily Singles Chart in Japan. In May, they released _Hit The Road_, a documentary series showing behind-the-scenes moments from their Ode to You tour.

[![Image 7: SEVENTEEN(세븐틴) - 'Ready to love' 응원법 3m 25s](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/a/ac/SEVENTEEN%28%EC%84%B8%EB%B8%90%ED%8B%B4%29_-_%27Ready_to_love%27_%EC%9D%91%EC%9B%90%EB%B2%95_3m_25s.jpg/300px-SEVENTEEN%28%EC%84%B8%EB%B8%90%ED%8B%B4%29_-_%27Ready_to_love%27_%EC%9D%91%EC%9B%90%EB%B2%95_3m_25s.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:SEVENTEEN(%EC%84%B8%EB%B8%90%ED%8B%B4)_-_%27Ready_to_love%27_%EC%9D%91%EC%9B%90%EB%B2%95_3m_25s.jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:SEVENTEEN(%EC%84%B8%EB%B8%90%ED%8B%B4)_-_%27Ready_to_love%27_%EC%9D%91%EC%9B%90%EB%B2%95_3m_25s.jpg "Enlarge")

 Seventeen performing a chant for "Ready to Love" in 2021.

On June 22, Seventeen released their seventh mini-album, _Heng:garæ_. It sold one million copies in less than a week, making Seventeen "million sellers." They also became the first international male artists in over 12 years to have an album top the Oricon Weekly Album Chart for two weeks. In October, they released their special album _Semicolon_. To promote their song "Home;Run," the group performed on CBS' _[The Late Late Show with James Corden](link_15)_, marking their US television debut.

In 2021, Seventeen released their third Japanese single, "Not Alone". In May, they announced their "Power of Love" project and their ninth mini-album, _Your Choice_. They also signed with [Geffen Records](link_6) and [Universal Music Group](link_7) for their music distribution in the US and internationally. On July 19, Pledis Entertainment announced that all members of Seventeen had renewed their contracts, showing their strong teamwork. Their eighth mini-album, _Attacca_, was released in October and sold two million copies.

### New Albums and World Tours (2022–2023)

On April 15, 2022, Seventeen released their first English digital single, "Darl+ing". This was a preview for their fourth studio album, _Face the Sun_, which came out on May 27 with the song "Hot". They also released their first film, _Seventeen Power of Love: The Movie_, in theaters worldwide.

[![Image 8: Seventeen BeTS Seoul 220625](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/a/a7/Seventeen_BeTS_Seoul_220625.png/300px-Seventeen_BeTS_Seoul_220625.png)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Seventeen_BeTS_Seoul_220625.png)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Seventeen_BeTS_Seoul_220625.png "Enlarge")

 Seventeen performing in Seoul during the Be The Sun tour, June 2022.

In May 2022, Pledis Entertainment announced the Be The Sun World Tour, Seventeen's third world tour. It started in Seoul in June and then went to 12 cities across the US and Canada. They also performed in Jakarta, Bangkok, Manila, Singapore, and six dome stadiums in Japan.

On July 18, 2022, Seventeen released _Sector 17_, a repackaged version of their fourth studio album. Its lead single was "_World." In November, they released their third Japanese mini-album, _Dream_. They also performed at the LA3C festival in Los Angeles, their first appearance at an American festival.

On April 24, 2023, Seventeen released their eleventh Korean mini-album, _FML_. This album broke records with 4.6 million pre-orders and became the best-selling album in history, selling 3.9 million copies on its first day. It included two main songs, "Super" and "F*ck My Life."

In July 2023, Seventeen started their Follow Tour with two concerts in Seoul. The tour then went to five cities in Japan, and later expanded to Bangkok, Bulacan, and Macau. They also released a Japanese "best of" album called _Always Yours_ in August. Their twelfth mini-album, _Seventeenth Heaven_, released on October 23, had over 5.2 million pre-orders, making it the most pre-ordered K-pop album ever. The song "God of Music" from this album became their first to reach number one on South Korea's Circle Digital Chart. In November, the group won their first "Daesang" (grand prize) for Album of the Year at the MAMA Awards.

### Celebrating 10 Years and New Adventures (2024–Present)

On January 6, 2024, Seventeen won three major awards at the Golden Disc Awards. Later that month, they made history as the first K-pop group to perform a concert at the [Philippine Sports Stadium](link_16) i

## M ind-blowing F acts

[![Image 5: Pillars of creation 2014 HST WFC3-UVIS full-res denoised](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/6/68/Pillars_of_creation_2014_HST_WFC3-UVIS_full-res_denoised.jpg/300px-Pillars_of_creation_2014_HST_WFC3-UVIS_full-res_denoised.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Pillars_of_creation_2014_HST_WFC3-UVIS_full-res_denoised.jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Pillars_of_creation_2014_HST_WFC3-UVIS_full-res_denoised.jpg "Enlarge")

 The Pillars of Creation in the [Eagle Nebula](link_35), one of the most famous space photographs in history taken by the Hubble Space Telescope.

**When the [Hubble Space Telescope](link_36) first opened its robotic eyes in 1990, scientists were shocked to see that every picture came out blurry.**

What had gone wrong? Hubble's giant main mirror had been polished into the wrong shape by a mistake smaller than 1/50th the thickness of a human hair! That tiny error was too small to see, but it was big enough to keep light from focusing correctly.

 Thankfully, astronomers and engineers did not give up. In December 1993, a brave crew of astronauts flew into space aboard the [Space Shuttle Endeavour](link_37) on a daring repair mission. During five intense spacewalks, they installed a special tool called COSTAR, which stands for Corrective Optics Space Telescope Axial Replacement. COSTAR worked like a pair of high-tech eyeglasses for Hubble, fixing its blurry vision. When Hubble looked back at the stars, everything was perfectly clear!

# Jun (Chinese entertainer) facts for kids

[Kids Encyclopedia Facts](https://kids.kiddle.co/)

**Wen Junhui** (born June 10, 1996), who is better known by his stage name **Jun**, is a Chinese singer, dancer, and actor. He is famous for being a member of the popular South Korean boy band [Seventeen](https://kids.kiddle.co/Seventeen_(South_Korean_band) "Seventeen (South Korean band)"). He works in both South Korea and his home country of China.

Before joining Seventeen, Jun was a child actor. He starred in several movies, including _The Pye Dog_ (2007) and _The Legend Is Born: Ip Man_ (2010). In 2023, he returned to acting as the main star in the show _Exclusive Fairytale_.

Besides his work with Seventeen, Jun has also released his own songs in Chinese, his native language. His songs "Limbo" and "Psycho" have been very successful. He even won the New Singer-Songwriter of the Year award at the Tencent Music Entertainment Awards for "Limbo."

## Contents

## Early Life and Dreams

Wen Junhui was born on June 10, 1996, in Shenzhen, China. As a child, he learned [wushu](https://kids.kiddle.co/Wushu_(sport) "Wushu (sport)"), a type of Chinese martial art. He dreamed of becoming a martial arts actor like his hero, [Jackie Chan](https://kids.kiddle.co/Jackie_Chan "Jackie Chan"). Jun also learned to play the piano and sometimes performs his own versions of Seventeen's songs.

## Career Journey

### From Child Actor to Teen Star

Jun started his career very early. When he was only two years old, he was in his first commercial. At age five, he appeared in the TV show _Dragon Laws_.

His role in the 2007 movie _The Pye Dog_ earned him a "New Performer of the Year" award from the Hong Kong Film Directors' Guild Awards. He was also nominated for Best New Performer at the 27th Hong Kong Film Awards. In 2010, he played the younger version of the famous martial artist [Ip Man](https://kids.kiddle.co/Ip_Man "Ip Man") in the movie _The Legend Is Born: Ip Man_.

### Becoming a Member of Seventeen

In 2012, Jun moved to South Korea to train with Pledis Entertainment. For three years, he practiced dancing and singing to prepare for his debut. He appeared on shows like _Seventeen TV_ with his future bandmates.

On May 26, 2015, he officially debuted as Jun, a member of the boy band [Seventeen](https://kids.kiddle.co/Seventeen_(South_Korean_band) "Seventeen (South Korean band)"). The group is split into three units, and Jun is part of the "performance team," which focuses on dancing. The group's first mini-album, _17 Carat_, was released just three days after their debut.

In 2018, Jun and his bandmate [The8](https://kids.kiddle.co/The8 "The8") competed in a Chinese music show called _Chao Yin Zhan Ji_. Jun won the first solo competition on the show with his performance of "Wo Ming Bai," a Chinese version of Seventeen's song "Thanks." He even wrote the Chinese lyrics himself.

### Going Solo and Other Projects

[![Image 4: Seventeen Jun Psycho](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/d/d7/Seventeen_Jun_Psycho.png/240px-Seventeen_Jun_Psycho.png)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Seventeen_Jun_Psycho.png)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Seventeen_Jun_Psycho.png "Enlarge")

 Jun in the music video for his solo song "Psycho" in 2023.

Jun began releasing his own music in 2018 with the song "Can You Sit By My Side." In 2021, he released two more singles, "Crow" and "Silent Boarding Gate." "Crow" was so popular that it appeared on the _Billboard_ World Digital Song Sales chart, which was a huge achievement for him as a solo artist.

In 2022, he released the single "Limbo" in both Korean and Chinese. A year later, he released another hit single, "Psycho." For his music, he won the "New Singer-Songwriter of the Year" award at the Tencent Music Entertainment Awards in 2023.

Jun returned to acting in 2023 with the lead role in the drama _Exclusive Fairytale_. His performance won him the Rising Star of the Year Award at the 2023 Asia Contents Awards & Global OTT Awards.

In August 2024, it was announced that Jun would take a break from some of Seventeen's activities to focus on acting in China. He later starred in the movie _The Shadow's Edge_ with the famous actor [Jackie Chan](https://kids.kiddle.co/Jackie_Chan "Jackie Chan").

# Time (magazine) facts for kids

[Kids Encyclopedia Facts](https://kids.kiddle.co/)

Quick facts for kids  
_Time_[![Image 3: Time Magazine logo.svg](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/b/b3/Time_Magazine_logo.svg/180px-Time_Magazine_logo.svg.png)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Time_Magazine_logo.svg)

**Time** magazine is a very famous American [news magazine](https://kids.kiddle.co/News_magazine "News magazine"). It started in [New York City](https://kids.kiddle.co/New_York_City "New York City") on March 3, 1923. For almost 100 years, it came out every week. Since March 2020, it has been published every other week. One of its co-founders, [Henry Luce](https://kids.kiddle.co/Henry_Luce "Henry Luce"), was very important in running the magazine for many years.

**Time** magazine also has different versions for other parts of the world. There's a European edition, called _Time Europe_, which covers Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and Latin America. It's published in [London](https://kids.kiddle.co/London "London"). There's also an Asian edition, _Time Asia_, based in Hong Kong. For Australia, [New Zealand](https://kids.kiddle.co/New_Zealand "New Zealand"), and the [Pacific Islands](https://kids.kiddle.co/List_of_islands_in_the_Pacific_Ocean "List of islands in the Pacific Ocean"), there's a South Pacific edition based in [Sydney](https://kids.kiddle.co/Sydney "Sydney").

Since 2018, Marc Benioff, who started the company Salesforce, has owned _Time_ magazine. He bought it from another company called Meredith Corporation.

## Contents

*   [Who is _Time'_ s Person of the Year?](https://kids.kiddle.co/Time_(magazine)#Who_is_Time.27s_Person_of_the_Year.3F)
*   [_Time for Kids_: A Magazine for Young Readers](https://kids.kiddle.co/Time_(magazine)#Time_for_Kids:_A_Magazine_for_Young_Readers)
*   [Images for kids](https://kids.kiddle.co/Time_(magazine)#Images_for_kids)
*   [See also](https://kids.kiddle.co/Time_(magazine)#See_also)

## Who is _Time'_ s Person of the Year?

[![Image 5: Charles Lindbergh Time cover 1928](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/4/48/Charles_Lindbergh_Time_cover_1928.jpg/300px-Charles_Lindbergh_Time_cover_1928.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Charles_Lindbergh_Time_cover_1928.jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Charles_Lindbergh_Time_cover_1928.jpg "Enlarge")

 1927 _Time_ Man of the Year cover featuring [Charles Lindbergh](https://kids.kiddle.co/Charles_Lindbergh "Charles Lindbergh"), the award's first winner.

Main article: [Time Person of the Year](https://kids.kiddle.co/Time_Person_of_the_Year "Time Person of the Year")

One of the most well-known things about _Time_ magazine is its yearly "Person of the Year" special. This used to be called "Man of the Year." Each year, _Time_ chooses a person or a group of people who have had the biggest influence on the news during the past 12 months.

The idea is to pick someone who, whether for good or bad reasons, has most changed the year's events. So, it's not always an award or an honor. For example, in the past, people like [Adolf Hitler](https://kids.kiddle.co/Adolf_Hitler "Adolf Hitler") and [Joseph Stalin](https://kids.kiddle.co/Joseph_Stalin "Joseph Stalin") were named "Man of the Year."

## _Time for Kids_: A Magazine for Young Readers

Main article: [_Time for Kids_](https://kids.kiddle.co/Time_for_Kids "Time for Kids")

_[Time for Kids](https://kids.kiddle.co/Time\_for\_Kids "Time for Kids")_ is a special magazine made by _Time_ just for children. It's mostly given out in classrooms at school. _Time for Kids_ includes some national news, a "[Cartoon](https://kids.kiddle.co/Cartoon "Cartoon") of the Week," and fun articles about popular culture. Every year, there's a special issue about the [environment](https://kids.kiddle.co/Natural_environment "Natural environment") that comes out near the end of the school year in the U.S. This magazine is usually not very long, often less than ten pages.

# Homework facts for kids

[Kids Encyclopedia Facts](https://kids.kiddle.co/)

[![Image 3: Child calculating with fingers](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/5/51/Child_calculating_with_fingers.jpg/300px-Child_calculating_with_fingers.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Child_calculating_with_fingers.jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Child_calculating_with_fingers.jpg "Enlarge")

 Homework

**Homework** is school work that students are given by their teachers to do at home. It's like practice that helps students remember what they learned in class. It also helps them review topics.

The amount of homework students get can be different. It usually depends on how old they are and what grade they are in. Older students often get more homework than younger ones.

[![Image 4: Homework - vector maths](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/1/15/Homework_-_vector_maths.jpg/300px-Homework_-_vector_maths.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Homework_-_vector_maths.jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Homework_-_vector_maths.jpg "Enlarge")

 Homework can include math problems

Teachers give homework for many reasons, including:

*   **Practice:** To help you practice what you learned.
*   **Preparation:** To get you ready for new topics.
*   **Participation:** To involve you more in your learning.
*   **Personal development:** To help you grow and learn on your own.
*   **Parent–child relations:** To give parents a chance to see what you're learning.
*   **Parent–teacher communications:** To help teachers and parents talk about your progress.
*   **Peer interactions:** Sometimes, homework involves working with classmates.

Homework can also help you learn how to be organized. It teaches you to work on tasks by yourself. It can also improve your time management and focus skills.

## Contents

*   [How Homework Affects Students](https://kids.kiddle.co/Homework#How_Homework_Affects_Students)

    *   [In the United Kingdom](https://kids.kiddle.co/Homework#In_the_United_Kingdom)

*   [Images for kids](https://kids.kiddle.co/Homework#Images_for_kids)

## How Homework Affects Students

### School Performance

[![Image 5: L’éducation](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/b/be/L%E2%80%99%C3%A9ducation.jpg/300px-L%E2%80%99%C3%A9ducation.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:L%E2%80%99%C3%A9ducation.jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:L%E2%80%99%C3%A9ducation.jpg "Enlarge")

 A child in Senegal doing homework

People have different ideas about whether homework really helps students do better in school. What studies show can change based on things like the students' age and how "academic performance" is measured.

Some studies suggest that homework doesn't always improve grades for younger students in elementary school. However, some people who support homework say it helps kids learn good study habits. But there isn't much research to prove this idea.

For teenagers, spending more time on homework often leads to higher grades and better test scores. But there's a limit! Studies have shown that if teenagers spend more than 90 minutes a day on homework, their school performance can actually get worse.

Interestingly, students who are struggling in school often benefit more from doing homework than those who are already doing well. However, teachers sometimes give less homework to students who need it most. They might give more homework to students who are already performing well. In the past, homework could even make students drop out of school. If they couldn't keep up with the work, they might just quit.

### Other Effects

The amount of homework you get doesn't always change how you feel about homework or school in general.

Some research suggests that homework can help students become more motivated and improve their study skills. In one study, parents and teachers thought homework helped middle school students learn to be responsible. However, the students themselves often felt negatively about homework. They were less likely to think it helped them develop these skills. Other studies found that students often felt negative emotions when doing homework. They were also less engaged compared to other activities.

## A Look Back: The History of Homework

[![Image 6: Homework in Japan, Taisho era (1915 by Elstner Hilton)](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/8/8e/Homework_in_Japan%2C_Taisho_era_%281915_by_Elstner_Hilton%29.jpg/300px-Homework_in_Japan%2C_Taisho_era_%281915_by_Elstner_Hilton%29.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Homework_in_Japan,_Taisho_era_(1915_by_Elstner_Hilton).jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Homework_in_Japan,_Taisho_era_(1915_by_Elstner_Hilton).jpg "Enlarge")

 Japanese students doing homework, around 1915

[![Image 7: Yrjö Ollila - Hearing the Homework](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/f/f9/Yrj%C3%B6_Ollila_-_Hearing_the_Homework.jpg/300px-Yrj%C3%B6_Ollila_-_Hearing_the_Homework.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Yrj%C3%B6_Ollila_-_Hearing_the_Homework.jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Yrj%C3%B6_Ollila_-_Hearing_the_Homework.jpg "Enlarge")

_Hearing the Homework_; a painting by Yrjö Ollila

### In the United States

For a long time, many people in the United States didn't like homework. Not many students went on to college back then. Also, many children and teenagers had to spend a lot of time doing chores or farm work. So, homework was unpopular with both parents and some schools. If students couldn't keep up with homework, which often meant memorizing texts at home, they might drop out of school early. Going to school wasn't always required by law.

Parents often complained about homework. In 1880, a man named Francis Amasa Walker convinced the school board in Boston to stop teachers from giving math homework. In 1900, a journalist named Edward Bok argued against giving homework to students under 15. He told parents to send notes to teachers demanding an end to homework, and thousands did! People also pointed out that school time plus homework could be more hours than a child was allowed to work for pay under new child labor laws. This led to experts telling the US Congress that children should never have homework. They also said teenagers should have no more than two hours of homework a day. In 1901, California even passed a law that basically got rid of homework for anyone under 15.

While homework wasn't popular in the first half of the 1900s, some people wanted to change it instead of banning it. They thought homework should be more connected to students' real lives outside of school.

In the 1950s, homework became popular again. This was because the United States wanted to stay ahead during the Cold War. Children were encouraged to keep up with students in the Soviet Union. Since then, attitudes about homework have changed every 15 years or so. It was popular from the 1950s to mid-1960s, then less popular until 1980. It became popular again from 1980 until the mid-1990s, when the Cold War ended. After the Cold War, homework became less favored again.

### In the United Kingdom

Students in the United Kingdom tend to get more homework than many other countries in Europe. On average, they spend about 5 hours a week on homework. There's also a difference in the UK based on social class. Middle-class teenagers often get a lot more homework compared to students in Asia and other parts of Europe.

### In Spain

In 2012, a report showed that children in Spain spend about 6.4 hours a week on homework.

**Hansol Vernon Chwe** ([Korean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_language "Korean language"):최한솔; born February 18, 1998), known [mononymously](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mononymously "Mononymously") as **Vernon** (버논), is a South Korean[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vernon_(rapper)#cite_note-1) and American[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vernon_(rapper)#cite_note-2) rapper, singer and songwriter. Managed by [Pledis Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pledis_Entertainment "Pledis Entertainment"), he is a member of the South Korean boy band [Seventeen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seventeen_(South_Korean_band) "Seventeen (South Korean band)"), its hip hop team, and the sub-unit [V8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V8_(duo) "V8 (duo)").

Vernon made his official solo debut with "Black Eye" on December 27, 2022. Aside from his work with Seventeen and as a soloist, he has written and produced music with and for other artists such as [Jamie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamie_(singer) "Jamie (singer)"), [Bumzu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bumzu "Bumzu"), and [Charli XCX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charli_XCX "Charli XCX").

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vernon_(rapper)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Hansol Vernon Chwe[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vernon_(rapper)#cite_note-teenvogue-3) was born at [Tisch Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tisch_Hospital "Tisch Hospital")[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vernon_(rapper)#cite_note-4) in [Kips Bay, Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kips_Bay,_Manhattan "Kips Bay, Manhattan"), [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") on February 18, 1998,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vernon_(rapper)#cite_note-5) to a Korean father and an American mother. At the age of five, he moved with his family to [Hongdae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hongdae_(area) "Hongdae (area)"), South Korea. He attended Changcheon Middle School but later opted for homeschooling with his parents after being scouted by Pledis, to focus on his training.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vernon_(rapper)#cite_note-teenvogue-3)

His stage name comes from his middle name, Vernon, which is also his mother's [maiden name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maiden_name "Maiden name").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vernon_(rapper)#cite_note-6) Both his parents are artists.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vernon_(rapper)#cite_note-weverse-7)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vernon_(rapper)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

### 2012–2014: Pre-debut

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vernon_(rapper)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 2012–2014: Pre-debut")]

Vernon joined [Pledis Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pledis_Entertainment "Pledis Entertainment") in 2012, after being scouted on the street, and received training for the next three years. Beginning in 2013, he participated in _[Seventeen TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seventeen\_TV "Seventeen TV")_, an online reality show that introduced Pledis' trainees and showed potential members of the boy group [Seventeen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seventeen_(South_Korean_band) "Seventeen (South Korean band)") before their official debut. The show was broadcast periodically on [Ustream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ustream "Ustream"), where the trainees showed themselves training, singing, creating choreographies, and playing games.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vernon_(rapper)#cite_note-8) The online show also included participation in concerts, such as Like Seventeen.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vernon_(rapper)#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vernon_(rapper)#cite_note-debut-10)

Before his official debut as an idol, Vernon made multiple appearances on South Korean television, including [Munhwa Broadcasting Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munhwa_Broadcasting_Corporation "Munhwa Broadcasting Corporation")'s _Hello Stranger!_, a program about foreigners in South Korea,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vernon_(rapper)#cite_note-hs-11) and [Song Eun-i](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Song_Eun-i "Song Eun-i")'s _Eye to Eye_, where he appeared as an elementary school student who was an expert in dating.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vernon_(rapper)#cite_note-e2e-12)

### 2015–present: Seventeen, solo activities and sub-unit activities

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Vernon_(rapper)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 2015–present: Seventeen, solo activities and sub-unit activities")]

In 2015, Vernon debuted as a member of the South Korean boy group [Seventeen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seventeen_(South_Korean_band) "Seventeen (South Korean band)") with the [extended play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extended_play "Extended play")_[17 Carat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/17\_Carat "17 Carat")_ o

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

(Redirected from [Eponymous](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Eponymous&redirect=no "Eponymous"))

Person or thing after which something is named

"Eponymous" redirects here. For the album, see [_Eponymous_ (album)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eponymous_(album) "Eponymous (album)")."Self-titled" redirects here. For other uses, see [Self-titled (disambiguation)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-titled_(disambiguation) "Self-titled (disambiguation)").Not to be confused with [Namesake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Namesake "Namesake").

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/47/Orion_Head_to_Toe.jpg/250px-Orion_Head_to_Toe.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Orion_Head_to_Toe.jpg)

The mythological Greek hero [Orion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orion_(mythology) "Orion (mythology)") is the eponym of the [constellation Orion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orion_(constellation) "Orion (constellation)"), shown here, and thus indirectly of the [Orion spacecraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orion_(spacecraft) "Orion (spacecraft)").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eponymous#cite_note-1)

An **eponym** is a [person](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Person "Person") or thing after which someone or something is named.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eponymous#cite_note-2) For example, [John Montagu, 4th Earl of Sandwich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Montagu,_4th_Earl_of_Sandwich "John Montagu, 4th Earl of Sandwich"), is the eponym of the [sandwich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandwich "Sandwich"). Adjectives derived from the word _eponym_ include _eponymous_ and _eponymic_.

Eponyms are commonly used for time periods, places, innovations, biological nomenclature, astronomical objects, works of art and media, and tribal names. Various orthographic conventions are used for eponyms.

## Usage of the word

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Eponym&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Usage of the word")]

The term _eponym_[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eponymous#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eponymous#cite_note-OED-4) functions in multiple related ways, all based on an explicit relationship between named people, places or things. _Eponym_ refers to a person, a place or a thing after which someone or something is named; or that someone or something. Such things share an eponymous relationship. In this way, [Elizabeth I of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_I_of_England "Elizabeth I of England") is the eponym of the [Elizabethan era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabethan_era "Elizabethan era"), but the [Elizabethan era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabethan_era "Elizabethan era") can also be referred to as the eponym of [Elizabeth I of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_I_of_England "Elizabeth I of England"). Eponyms may be named for things or places, for example [Downing Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downing_Street "Downing Street") in London is named for [Sir George Downing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_George_Downing,_1st_Baronet "Sir George Downing, 1st Baronet"), who had the houses built there as an investment: However, Downing never lived in his eponymous street.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eponymous#cite_note-Jones-5) Adjectives and verbs may be eponyms, for example _[bowdlerize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowdlerize "Bowdlerize")_.

Adjectives derived from the word eponym include _eponymous_ and _eponymic_. When [Henry Ford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Ford "Henry Ford") is referred to as "the _eponymous_ founder of the [Ford Motor Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ford_Motor_Company "Ford Motor Company")", his surname "Ford" and the name of the motor company have an eponymous relationship. The word "eponym" can also refer to the [title character](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Title_character "Title character") of a fictional work (such as [Rocky Balboa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocky_Balboa "Rocky Balboa") of the [_Rocky_ film series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocky_film_series "Rocky film series")), as well as to _**self-titled**_ works named after their creators (such as the album [_The Doors_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doors_(album) "The Doors (album)") by the band [the Doors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doors "The Doors")).

[Walt Disney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walt_Disney "Walt Disney") created the eponymous [Walt Disney Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Walt_Disney_Company "The Walt Disney Company"), with his name similarly extended to theme parks such as [Walt Disney World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walt_Disney_World "Walt Disney World").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eponymous#cite_note-dictionary_com_eponym-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eponymous#cite_note-m-w_eponym-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eponymous#cite_note-dictionary_com_eponymous-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eponymous#cite_note-m-w_eponymous-9) Medical eponymous terms are often called [medical eponyms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lists_of_medical_eponyms "Lists of medical eponyms"), regardless of that usage being [deprecated](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/deprecated#English "wikt:deprecated") by those speakers who wish to reserve the term _eponym_ to the person.

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Eponym&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/03/Voices_by_Alice_in_Chains_%28Single-CD%29_%28US-2013%29.jpg/250px-Voices_by_Alice_in_Chains_%28Single-CD%29_%28US-2013%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Voices_by_Alice_in_Chains_(Single-CD)_(US-2013).jpg)

In [music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_industry "Music industry"), a **single** is a type of [release](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_release#Music "Art release") of a song [recording](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sound_recording "Sound recording") of fewer tracks than an [album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album "Album") ([LP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LP_record "LP record")).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single_(music)#cite_note-Emubands-1) As the name suggests, a single typically contains only a single song, but they can sometimes have two.

A single can be released for [sale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Record_sales "Record sales") to the public in a variety of physical or digital formats. Singles may be standalone tracks or connected to an artist's album, and in the latter case would often have at least one single release before the album itself, called [lead singles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lead_single "Lead single").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single_(music)#cite_note-Leight-2)

The single was defined in the mid-20th century with the _45_ (named after its speed in [revolutions per minute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revolutions_per_minute "Revolutions per minute")), a type of 7-inch sized [vinyl record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vinyl_records "Vinyl records") containing an [A-side and a B-side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A-side_and_B-side "A-side and B-side"), i.e. one song on each side.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single_(music)#cite_note-3) The single format was highly influential in [pop music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_music "Pop music") and the early days of [rock and roll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_roll "Rock and roll"), and it was the format used for [jukeboxes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jukeboxes "Jukeboxes") and preferred by younger populations in the 1950s and 1960s.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single_(music)#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single_(music)#cite_note-Browne-5)

Singles in [digital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_distribution "Digital distribution") form became very popular in the 2000s.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single_(music)#cite_note-6) Distinctions for what makes a _single_ have become more tenuous since the biggest [digital music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_music "Digital music") distributor, the [iTunes Store](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ITunes_Store "ITunes Store"), only accepts as singles releases with three tracks or fewer that are less than ten minutes each (with longer releases being classified as _[EPs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EPs "EPs")_ or _albums_).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single_(music)#cite_note-Emubands-1) However, releases which do not fit these criteria have been promoted as singles by artists and labels elsewhere, such as on [Spotify](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spotify "Spotify") and the [Bandcamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bandcamp "Bandcamp") storefront.

Nowadays physically released music is mainly bought in the form of albums instead of singles.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single_(music)#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single_(music)#cite_note-8) The most

# K-pop facts for kids

[Kids Encyclopedia Facts](https://kids.kiddle.co/)

| Cultural origins | Mid to late 1990s, [South Korea](https://kids.kiddle.co/South_Korea "South Korea") |
| Typical instruments | [Vocals](https://kids.kiddle.co/Singing "Singing") • [Drum pad](https://kids.kiddle.co/Drum_machine "Drum machine") • [Drums](https://kids.kiddle.co/Drum_kit "Drum kit") • [Electric bass](https://kids.kiddle.co/Bass_guitar "Bass guitar") • [Keyboards](https://kids.kiddle.co/Keyboard_instrument "Keyboard instrument") • [Piano](https://kids.kiddle.co/Piano "Piano") • Sampler • [Sequencer](https://kids.kiddle.co/Music_sequencer "Music sequencer") • [Synthesizer](https://kids.kiddle.co/Synthesizer "Synthesizer") • Occasional use of various other [instruments](https://kids.kiddle.co/Musical_instrument "Musical instrument") |

**K-pop** (short for **Korean pop**) is a popular music style from [South Korea](https://kids.kiddle.co/South_Korea "South Korea"). It uses many different sounds and visuals. While K-pop has been around since the early 1990s, the name "K-pop" became very popular in the 2000s. Before that, people often called Korean pop music "Gayo."

K-pop usually means "popular music" in South Korea. But it also describes a newer type of Korean pop music. This modern K-pop mixes styles from all over the world. It includes sounds like [jazz](https://kids.kiddle.co/Jazz "Jazz"), [hip hop](https://kids.kiddle.co/Hip_hop "Hip hop"), [R&B](https://kids.kiddle.co/Contemporary_R%26B "Contemporary R&B"), [reggae](https://kids.kiddle.co/Reggae "Reggae"), and [electronic dance](https://kids.kiddle.co/Electronic_dance_music "Electronic dance music"). It also keeps some of its unique traditional Korean music roots.

The modern K-pop sound really started with the group [Seo Taiji and Boys](https://kids.kiddle.co/Seo_Taiji_and_Boys "Seo Taiji and Boys") in 1992. They tried out many different music styles. They also added foreign music elements. This helped to change and update South Korea's music scene.

The idea of K-pop "idols" began with the boy band [H.O.T.](https://kids.kiddle.co/H.O.T._(band) "H.O.T. (band)") in 1996. K-pop then grew into a big [subculture](https://kids.kiddle.co/Subculture "Subculture"). It gained huge fan groups of teenagers and young adults. After a quiet period for K-pop, groups like [TVXQ](https://kids.kiddle.co/TVXQ "TVXQ") and [BoA](https://kids.kiddle.co/BoA "BoA") started a new wave of idols in 2003. These artists helped K-pop become popular in Japan. They continue to make K-pop famous around the world today.

Thanks to online [social networking services](https://kids.kiddle.co/Social_networking_service "Social networking service") and Korean TV shows, K-pop is now known globally. This spread of Korean entertainment is called the Korean Wave. You can see it not just in [East](https://kids.kiddle.co/East_Asia "East Asia") and [Southeast Asia](https://kids.kiddle.co/Southeast_Asia "Southeast Asia"), but also in [Latin America](https://kids.kiddle.co/Latin_America "Latin America"), [India](https://kids.kiddle.co/India "India"), [North Africa](https://kids.kiddle.co/North_Africa "North Africa"), the [Middle East](https://kids.kiddle.co/Middle_East "Middle East"), and the [Western world](https://kids.kiddle.co/Western_world "Western world"). K-pop now has a huge audience worldwide.

## How K-Pop Artists Train

[![Image 5: 실용음악학과 K-POP 신한류 뮤직페스티벌 결선 현장! (11)](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/d/d5/%EC%8B%A4%EC%9A%A9%EC%9D%8C%EC%95%85%ED%95%99%EA%B3%BC_K-POP_%EC%8B%A0%ED%95%9C%EB%A5%98_%EB%AE%A4%EC%A7%81%ED%8E%98%EC%8A%A4%ED%8B%B0%EB%B2%8C_%EA%B2%B0%EC%84%A0_%ED%98%84%EC%9E%A5%21_%2811%29.jpg/300px-%EC%8B%A4%EC%9A%A9%EC%9D%8C%EC%95%85%ED%95%99%EA%B3%BC_K-POP_%EC%8B%A0%ED%95%9C%EB%A5%98_%EB%AE%A4%EC%A7%81%ED%8E%98%EC%8A%A4%ED%8B%B0%EB%B2%8C_%EA%B2%B0%EC%84%A0_%ED%98%84%EC%9E%A5%21_%2811%29.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:%EC%8B%A4%EC%9A%A9%EC%9D%8C%EC%95%85%ED%95%99%EA%B3%BC_K-POP_%EC%8B%A0%ED%95%9C%EB%A5%98_%EB%AE%A4%EC%A7%81%ED%8E%98%EC%8A%A4%ED%8B%B0%EB%B2%8C_%EA%B2%B0%EC%84%A0_%ED%98%84%EC%9E%A5!_(11).jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:%EC%8B%A4%EC%9A%A9%EC%9D%8C%EC%95%85%ED%95%99%EA%B3%BC_K-POP_%EC%8B%A0%ED%95%9C%EB%A5%98_%EB%AE%A4%EC%A7%81%ED%8E%98%EC%8A%A4%ED%8B%B0%EB%B2%8C_%EA%B2%B0%EC%84%A0_%ED%98%84%EC%9E%A5!_(11).jpg "Enlarge")

 Students at a K-pop music festival in 2017

Music companies in South Korea offer special contracts to young artists. Sometimes, these artists are very young when they start. Trainees live together and follow a strict schedule. They spend many hours each day learning music, dance, and foreign languages. They also learn other skills to get ready for their debut. Some people in Western media criticize this strict training system. In 2012, _[The Wall Street Journal](https://kids.kiddle.co/The\_Wall\_Street\_Journal "The Wall Street Journal")_ reported that training one Korean idol at [S.M. Entertainment](https://kids.kiddle.co/SM_Entertainment "SM Entertainment") cost about US$3 million.

K-pop is more than just music; it shares "values, identity and meanings." It mixes Western sounds with an Asian way of performing. Many believe K-pop's global success comes from its shared values. For example, K-pop idols are known for their high-quality performances. They also show a strong work ethic and polite behavior. This is all thanks to their long training period.

## Marketing K-Pop Groups

[![Image 6: Bobby - 2016 Gaon Chart K-pop Awards red carpet](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/f/f6/Bobby_-_2016_Gaon_Chart_K-pop_Awards_red_carpet.jpg/300px-Bobby_-_2016_Gaon_Chart_K-pop_Awards_red_carpet.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Bobby_-_2016_Gaon_Chart_K-pop_Awards_red_carpet.jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Bobby_-_2016_Gaon_Chart_K-pop_Awards_red_carpet.jpg "Enlarge")

 iKON's Bobby at the 2016 Gaon Chart K-pop Awards

Many K-pop companies introduce new idol groups with a "debut showcase." This means they use online videos and TV shows to promote the group. They don't usually use radio much at first. Groups are given a name and a "concept." This concept is the visual and musical theme they use when they first start or when they release new music. Concepts can change, and fans often see differences between boy group and girl group concepts.

Concepts can be general, like "cute" or "fantasy." New idol groups often start with a well-known concept to help them succeed. Sometimes, smaller groups called "sub-units" are formed from existing members. For example, Super Junior-K.R.Y. has members Kyuhyun, Ryeowook, and Yesung. [Super Junior-M](https://kids.kiddle.co/Super_Junior-M "Super Junior-M") became one of the most popular K-pop sub-groups in China.

Online marketing is very important. Music videos are posted on YouTube to reach fans all over the world.

## Amazing Choreography

[![Image 7: 2014 K-Pop Night Out at SXSW, Hyuna](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/2/2a/2014_K-Pop_Night_Out_at_SXSW%2C_Hyuna.JPG/300px-2014_K-Pop_Night_Out_at_SXSW%2C_Hyuna.JPG)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:2014_K-Pop_Night_Out_at_SXSW,_Hyuna.JPG)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:2014_K-Pop_Night_Out_at_SXSW,_Hyuna.JPG "Enlarge")

 Hyuna performing at K-Pop Night Out in 2014

Dance is a huge part of K-pop. When many singers perform together, they often switch places while singing and dancing. They make quick, synchronized movements. This is called "formation changing." K-pop [choreography](https://kids.kiddle.co/Choreography "Choreography") often includes a "point dance." This is a catchy, repeated dance move that matches the song's lyrics.

[Super Junior](https://kids.kiddle.co/Super_Junior "Super Junior")'s "Sorry Sorry" and Brown Eyed Girls' "Abracadabra" are famous for their "point" choreography. When choreographers create a dance, they must think about the song's speed. They also consider if fans can easily learn the steps. This means K-pop choreographers often simplify movements.

The training for K-pop idols to dance well is very intense. Dance schools like Seoul's Def Dance Skool help young people develop their dance skills. This gives them a chance to become an idol. Physical training is a big focus at these schools. Students spend much of their time dancing and exercising. Entertainment companies are very picky, so only a few make it to fame. Students must dedicate their lives to mastering dance. This prepares them for the tough routines K-pop groups perform. If they are chosen, the training continues with the company.

## K-Pop Fashion

[![Image 8: G-Dragon 2012 2](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/b/b9/G-Dragon_2012_2.jpg/300px-G-Dragon_2012_2.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:G-Dragon_2012_2.jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:G-Dragon_2012_2.jpg "Enlarge")

 G-Dragon performing on Alive World tour in 2012

K-pop has a big impact on fashion in Asia. Young fans often follow trends started by their favorite idols. Some idols, like G-Dragon and CL, are known as fashion icons. CL has even worked with famous designer [Jeremy Scott](https://kids.kiddle.co/Jeremy_Scott "Jeremy Scott").

There are some concerns about beauty trends popularized by the industry. For example, the focus on very pale skin has been criticized. This is because it promotes a narrow idea of beauty.

When [Seo Taiji and Boys](https://kids.kiddle.co/Seo_Taiji_and_Boys "Seo Taiji and Boys") started in 1992, they changed Korean music. They added [rap](https://kids.kiddle.co/Hip_hop "Hip hop") and American [hip-hop](https://kids.kiddle.co/Hip_hop "Hip hop") styles to their songs. This Western influence also showed in their clothes. The band wore hip-hop fashion. Many groups that came after them copied this style. Groups like Deux and DJ DOC also wore popular hip-hop clothes. They wore baggy pants, sportswear, and [bandanas](https://kids.kiddle.co/Bandana "Bandana").

[![Image 9: Seo Taiji on October 20, 2014 (1)](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/3/37/Seo_Taiji_on_October_20%2C_2014_%281%29.jpg/300px-Seo_Taiji_on_October_20%2C_2014_%281%29.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Seo_Taiji_on_October_20,_2014_(1).jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Seo_Taiji_on_October_20,_2014_(1).jpg "Enlarge")

 Seo Taiji in 2014

As Korean pop music became popular with young people, new idol groups appeared in the mid-to-late 1990s. They wore matching outfits that showed the popular youth fashion trends. Hip-hop fashion was very popular in the late 90s. Idol groups like [H.O.T.](https://kids.kiddle.co/H.O.T._(band) "H.O.T. (band)") and [Sechs Kies](https://kids.kiddle.co/Sechs_Kies "Sechs Kies") wore this style for their first songs. Accessories made the idols' style special for performances. They used ski goggles, headphones around their necks, and oversized gloves. These gloves helped make their dance moves stand out.

[H.O.T.](https://kids.kiddle.co/H.O.T._(band) "H.O.T. (band)")'s 1996 hit "Candy" shows how much thought went into idol costumes. Each member wore a specific color. They also used face paint, fuzzy mittens, visors, and earmuffs. They even used stuffed animals and backpacks as props. Male idol groups had similar colors and styles in their outfits. But each member's outfit still looked a bit different. Female idol groups in the 90s often wore very similar costumes. Their early outfits aimed to show an innocent and youthful image.

[![Image 10: Jun - 2016 Gaon Chart K-pop Awards red carpet](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/f/f8/Jun_-_2016_Gaon_Chart_K-pop_Awards_red_carpet.jpg/300px-Jun_-_2016_Gaon_Chart_K-pop_Awards_red_carpet.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Jun_-_2016_Gaon_Chart_K-pop_Awards_red_carpet.jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:Jun_-_2016_Gaon_Chart_K-pop_Awards_red_carpet.jpg "Enlarge")

 Jun at the Gaon Chart K-pop Awards in 2016

K-pop fashion has changed a lot over the years. The "ulzzang" style became popular with K-pop. This look includes big, delicate eyes, a tiny nose, and smooth, pale skin. A small, sharp chin to create a "V-line" face is also desired. This look is hard to get naturally. So, things like colored contact lenses, plastic surgeries, and skin-lightening products became popular. From the late 2000s, K-pop mixed Western and Asian cultures. This made fashion trends in K-pop very diverse. Here are some fashion trends from the late 2000s to early 2010s:

*   **Street:** This style focuses on being unique. It uses bright colors, mixed patterns, and graphic prints. Sports brands like Adidas and Reebok were common (e.g., 2NE1-Fire, SHINee-Ring Ding Dong).
*   **Retro:** This style brings back old looks from the 1960s to 1980s. It uses polka dots and detailed patterns. Common items include denim jackets, boot-cut pants, and scarves (e.g., Wonder Girls-Nobody, Tiara-Roly Poly).

[![Image 11: HyunA - 2014 Gaon Chart K-pop Awards red carpet](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/b/bf/HyunA_-_2014_Gaon_Chart_K-pop_Awards_red_carpet.jpg/300px-HyunA_-_2014_Gaon_Chart_K-pop_Awards_red_carpet.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:HyunA_-_2014_Gaon_Chart_K-pop_Awards_red_carpet.jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:HyunA_-_2014_Gaon_Chart_K-pop_Awards_red_carpet.jpg "Enlarge")

 HyunA on the red carpet of the Gaon Chart K-pop Awards in 2014

*   **Cute:** This style highlights being feminine or masculine. Outfits use satin, lace, fur, and leather. Common clothes are mini skirts, corsets, and high heels (e.g., Girls' Generation-The Boys, TVXQ-Mirotic).
*   **Black & White:** This style looks modern and chic. It shows elegance and charm. It is often used for formal wear (e.g., Girls' Generation-Genie, Super Junior-Sorry Sorry).
*   **Futurism:** This style is often seen with electronic and hip-hop music. It uses bright colors and metallic details. It aims to look like something from the future (e.g., 2NE1-I am the Best, NCT U-Seventh Sense).

## Government Support for K-Pop

[![Image 12: South Korean exports of cultural products and services](https://kids.kiddle.co/images/thumb/4/43/South_Korean_exports_of_cultural_products_and_services.jpg/300px-South_Korean_exports_of_cultural_products_and_services.jpg)](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:South_Korean_exports_of_cultural_products_and_services.jpg)

[](https://kids.kiddle.co/Image:South_Korean_exports_of_cultural_products_and_services.jpg "Enlarge")
